newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS-SIMEX Taiwan stock futures seen as useful hedge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SIMEX Taiwan stock futures seen as useful hedge.

text.p: Taiwan stock index futures made a disappointing debut on Singapore's futures exchange on Thursday with Taiwanese investors staying away, but the contract should attract growing interest as a hedging tool, traders said.

Interest in the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) Taiwan index futures contract was also dampened by the simultaneous launch of a separate Taiwan stock index contract on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), they said.

The March contract of the SIMEX Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) Taiwan index saw an estimated 500 lots change hands by the close. It settled at 307.3, against an opening 299.5, after reaching an early high of 311.
"Given that this is the start and it's a stock index, I'm a bit disappointed. I was hoping for at least 1,000 lots," said a trader with a local futures house.
He said most of the trades were "complimentary", reflected in the fact that the contract's movements did not follow the cash market.
Dealers attributed the bulk of market turnover to some commission house and local dealer orders. Locals are those who trade on their own account.
"The customer base is not there because of constraints on Taiwan investors," one foreign commission house dealer said.
"The simultaneous launch by Globex this morning has also affected liquidity."

Taiwan has not yet legalised trading by local investors of the Taiwan stock index futures contracts launched five minutes apart by both SIMEX and the CME on the GLOBEX after-hours electronic trading system.

Playing for time to build its own futures infrastructure, the country has stopped short of deeming the rivals hostile but has withheld technical cooperation and threatened to cut access to stock price data crucial to the SIMEX and CME indices.
SIMEX traders said they had received inquiries from Taiwanese investors, whom they expected to skirt the ban through "underground" offshore accounts.
"The initial margins are pretty low so I wouldn't be surprised if the Taiwanese are interested," said a trader at another local institution.

Desmond Supple, senior emerging markets economist at research firm I.D.E.A., said it was inevitable that Taiwanese and foreign investors would use the SIMEX and CME contracts as hedging instruments although they do not mirror the domestic stock exchange's Taiwan All Share Index (TAIEX).

"There is a very clear need for some form of hedging on the Taiwan stock market. In terms of market turnover, it's the world's sixth largest and foreign interest is rising as the government gradually liberalises foreign access," Supple said.
He said the market's volatility, a result of Taiwan's tense relations with mainland China, reinforced the need for investors to hedge their risk.

SIMEX officials said the MSCI Taiwan index, a market capitalisation-weighted index of 77 component stocks covering 67 percent of the Taiwan stock market, had an almost identical correlation with the TAIEX.
They said the contract was likely to succeed because it was traded during Asian time on an open outcry system.
SIMEX president Ang Swee Tian said the development of the exchange's Taiwan stock index futures and options would accelerate the internationalisation of Taiwan's stock market.
